title: November Update 18.12.0
body_markdown:
Released on **November 10, 2026**.

### IDE

**Work in Solution Explorer's File System view**
> *Browse your repository's physical layout, switch solutions, and run project commands from Solution Explorer's File System view.*
>
> Solution Explorer's **File System** view lets you explore your repository's physical layout while keeping solution and project actions within reach.
>
> ##### Browse your repository's physical layout
>
> Switch to **File System** view to browse files as they exist on disk, including documentation, build assets, and configuration files outside your projects. In a repository, the view starts at the repository root; otherwise, it starts at the solution folder. Switch back to **Solution** view for project structure, dependencies, and loaded projects.
>
> ![Solution Explorer showing the repository's File System view](media/18.12/se-filesystem-animation.gif)
>
> To keep both layouts visible, choose **New Solution Explorer View** from the context menu and put **Solution** and **File System** views side by side. You don't need a separate window merely to switch views.
>
> ##### Switch solutions from File System view
>
> If your repository contains several solutions, you can open another one without leaving its physical folder layout. Double-click a solution file in **File System** view, then choose whether to open it in your current Visual Studio instance or a new one.
>
> ![Solution switch dialog with Open and Open in a New Instance buttons](media/18.12/file-system-switch-solution.png)
>
> ##### Run project commands without switching views
>
> Right-click a project in **File System** view to use **Build**, **Rebuild**, **Clean**, or **Set as Startup Project**. You can explore files outside the solution and use common project commands from the same view.
>
> These actions apply to projects in the active solution. Projects outside that solution don't enable the build actions.
>
> ![File System view project menu with build and startup commands](media/18.12/solution-file-system-actions-2.png)


**Restore MSBuild dependencies in Open Folder**
> *Run MSBuild Restore from Open Folder without opening a solution first.*
>
> When you work in **Open Folder**, you can prepare MSBuild dependencies without opening a solution first. Right-click a supported solution or project file and choose **Restore** to run the MSBuild Restore target through the folder's existing build-action workflow.
>
> For a project that belongs to a discovered solution, the action preserves its solution-specific targeting. This keeps restore in the project's solution context even though you're working from the folder view.
>
> This action doesn't apply to CMake or other build providers, and excludes C++ `.vcxproj` files.
>
> ![Running Restore from an MSBuild project context menu in Open Folder](media/18.12/open-folder-msbuild-restore-1.gif)


**More settings in updated Options**
> *The updated Options experience includes product-update, Dev Containers, and graphics capture settings without resetting your preferences.*
>
> The updated Options experience brings more existing settings into the same interface without resetting your saved preferences.
>
> ##### Manage product updates
>
> Manage **Background Downloads**, **Operation Mode**, and supported **Update on Close** behavior in updated Options. Your existing defaults and saved choices remain, and the installer action is still available.
>
> Controls reflect product capabilities and organizational policy. If policy disables **Update on Close**, the page retains the explanation instead of presenting a setting you can change.
>
> ##### Find Dev Containers settings
>
> Open **Cross Platform â Dev Containers** in updated Options to manage existing container preferences. Your saved settings and host selection stay synchronized with the existing store; you don't need to recreate your container setup. This integration ships with the CMake Linux extension.
>
> ##### Configure graphics captures
>
> The seven existing graphics **Capture** controls now appear in updated Options. Compatibility mode and HUD options use positive labels, and the page updates when another process changes the shared capture values. The migrated page replaces the legacy placeholder rather than showing two competing pages.


**ANSI colors in the Output window ð£**
> *Render ANSI-colored tool output without raw escape sequences obscuring messages.*
>
> If a tool emits ANSI-colored messages, you can now read those colors directly in the **Output** window instead of seeing raw escape sequences mixed into the text.
>
> Enable colorized output in Visual Studio's visual-experience settings to try it. The option starts disabled, so you keep verbatim output until you choose color rendering.
>
> ![Output window displaying tool messages with ANSI colors](media/18.12/output-window-ansi-colors-1.png)
>
> When you enable the option, Visual Studio removes escape sequences from the displayed text and preserves their color transitions. Selection, copying, and searching then use the visible text, not the hidden sequences.
>
> Leave the option off if you need the original output exactly as the tool emitted it, including escape sequences.
>
> ð£ *See [feature ticket](https://developercommunity.visualstudio.com/idea/777436/colorized-output-window.html) to share your feedback and continue the conversation.*


**Read compact language-server hover tips ð£**
> *Language-server hover tips show syntax-colored signatures and examples in a compact view that covers less of your code.*
>
> Hover tips from language servers now show fenced code in compact, syntax-colored views instead of large generic panels. Signatures and examples take less space over the editor, and the prominent **Copy Code** control is removed.
>
> ![Compact Rust hover tip with a syntax-colored signature and example](media/18.12/compact-language-server-hover-after.png)
>
> Markdown links and keyboard navigation still work. The embedded code is a read-only display, not another editor that takes focus or offers text selection. This applies to language-server hover content, not every Quick Info provider.
>
> ð£ *See [feature ticket](https://developercommunity.visualstudio.com/t/The-JavaScriptTypeScript-Native-Languag/11150826) to share your feedback and continue the conversation.*


**Preview more image formats ð£**
> *Solution Explorer previews more image formats, including TIFF, DDS, and WebP, without opening an editor.*
>
> Hover over an image in Solution Explorer to preview TIFF, DDS, JPEG XR, HD Photo, Windows Media Photo, or WebP, alongside existing PNG, JPEG, GIF, BMP, and ICO support. Previews also work in **Open Folder**, matching the formats available in the editor.
>
> Some formats, including WebP, may require the appropriate Windows image codecs.
>
> ![Solution Explorer showing an image preview on hover](media/18.12/image-formats-thumbnail.png)
>
> ð£ *See [feature ticket](https://developercommunity.visualstudio.com/t/Solution-Explorer-image-hover-preview-la/11144795) to share your feedback and continue the conversation.*


**Tab and window management improvements ð£**
> *Customize tool-window tabs, close tabs to the right, and cancel accidental window drags.*
>
> ##### Customize tool-window tabs
>
> Choose how much space tool-window tabs can use by setting their minimum and maximum widths. Go to **Tools â Options â Environment â Tabs â Tool Window Tabs** to customize the limits.
>
> ![Tool Window Tabs settings for minimum and maximum tab widths](media/18.12/docked-tabs-min-max.png)
>
> **Before**
>
> ![Docked Tabs Before](media/18.12/docked-tabs-before.png)
>
> **After**
>
> ![Docked Tabs After](media/18.12/docked-tabs-after.png)
>
> Tool-window tabs shrink to their content size and your minimum width before truncating labels with an ellipsis and shrinking all tabs uniformly.
>
> ![Docked Tabs Shrink](media/18.12/docked-tabs-shrinking.gif)
>
> Tool-window tabs also use a consistent 24-pixel height, show clearer drag feedback, and improve high-contrast behavior.
>
> ##### Close tabs to the right
>
> Right-click a document tab or a tool window docked in the document well and select **Close Tabs to the Right**. With vertical tabs, choose **Close Tabs Below** instead. The command follows visible tab order, keeps pinned and unpinned groups separate, and leaves preview tabs open.
>
> ![Document-tab menu with Close Tabs to the Right](media/18.12/close-tabs-horizontal.png)
>
> ##### Cancel a window drag
>
> While dragging a docked window, press `Esc` before releasing the mouse button. Visual Studio cancels the drag and returns the window to its previous docked position.
>
> ð£ *See [feature ticket](https://developercommunity.visualstudio.com/t/Docked-window-tabs-should-have-individua/11010090) to share your feedback and continue the conversation.*


**Syntax highlighting and TextMate updates**
> *Read more file types with improved syntax highlighting and try a faster Preview TextMate matcher.*
>
> Visual Studio's editor improves syntax colors across more file types. TextMate matching also gains a separate Preview option.
>
> ##### Edit TOML and Rust with updated grammars
>
> TOML files now support syntax highlighting, code folding, brace completion, and comment/uncomment commands through a new TextMate grammar.
>
> ![TOML file with syntax highlighting in the Visual Studio editor](media/18.12/textmate-updates.png)
>
> The updated Rust TextMate grammar improves syntax highlighting and recognizes newer Rust language features.
>
> ##### Read registry and solution files more easily
>
> Registry (`.reg`) and package-definition (`.pkgdef`) files now highlight comments, sections, assignments, strings, deletion syntax, and typed values. Package-definition highlighting also recognizes `qword:` values and `#include` directives. Solution files gain highlighting for their structure too.
>
> ![Registry file with syntax-colored sections, strings, and numeric values](media/18.12/registry-solution-syntax-highlighting-2.png)
>
> ![Solution file with syntax-colored project and configuration sections](media/18.12/solution-file-syntax-coloring.png)
>
> ##### Try faster TextMate matching
>
> Enable **Use faster TextMate grammar matching** in **Preview Features** to try the new matcher. It searches eligible grammar rules together and keeps the existing matcher for unsupported cases.
>
> In a local benchmark using one 1.09 MB TypeScript fixture, parsing fell from 8.989 seconds to 1.882 seconds. This result describes that fixture, not a guaranteed improvement for every file. The matcher doesn't replace the JavaScript or TypeScript language service.

### Productivity

**Control inline suggestions in comments ð£**
> *Turn off automatic inline suggestions in comments without disabling them in code.*
>
> Turn off automatic inline suggestions in comments without disabling them in code. Open **Tools â Options â Text Editor â Preferences** and clear **Show suggestions in comments**.
>
> The preference starts enabled to preserve existing behavior and includes C# XML documentation and C++ comments. You can still explicitly request completion in a comment when you want it.
>
> ![Inline suggestions disabled while writing a comment](media/18.12/autocomplete-in-comments-thumbnail.png)
>
> ð£ *See [feature ticket](https://developercommunity.visualstudio.com/t/Turn-off-autocomplete-in-comments/10983048) to share your feedback and continue the conversation.*


**Follow line lengths with editor rulers ð£**
> *Display editor guides at configured columns to follow your repository's line-length conventions.*
>
> The editor adds line guides so you can follow your repository's configured line lengths while writing.
>
> ![Vertical ruler guides shown at configured column widths in the editor](media/18.12/max-length-ruler.gif)
>
> Use `rulers` to display one or more guides:
>
> ```
> rulers = 80, 120
> ```
>
> When `rulers` isn't specified, Visual Studio falls back to `max_line_length`:
>
> ```
> max_line_length = 120
> ```
>
> If both properties are present, `rulers` takes precedence. Set either property to `unset` to suppress an inherited value. The guide color follows the Visual Studio theme and can be customized through **Tools â Options â Environment â Fonts and Colors**.
>
> ð£ *See [feature ticket](https://developercommunity.visualstudio.com/t/support-max-line-length-in-editorconfig-for-visual/567214) to share your feedback and continue the conversation.*


**Markdown links and heading navigation ð£**
> *Create Markdown links by dragging files and follow links directly to headings in other documents.*
>
> Adding links and images to Markdown is now as easy as drag and drop. Drag a file from Solution Explorer or Windows File Explorer onto the Markdown editor, and Visual Studio inserts the correct Markdown syntax at the drop location. Regular files become links, while supported image files become image references.
>
> ![Drag and drop files onto markdown documents](media/18.12/markdown-drop-file-and-preview.gif)
>
> Visual Studio handles the path details for you. Links use paths relative to the current Markdown document, with normalized separators and encoded spaces, so they're portable across machines and ready to use immediately. The original file stays in place, so you can build documentation without interrupting your workflow.
>
> ##### Follow links to headings
>
> In the Markdown preview, follow a link such as `[Installation](setup.md#installation)` to open the target file and scroll both its editor and preview to the matching heading.
>
> This also works in a standalone preview. Visual Studio waits for the destination preview to finish rendering, including asynchronous content such as Mermaid diagrams, before scrolling to the heading.
>
> ð£ *See [feature ticket 1](https://developercommunity.visualstudio.com/t/Markdown-editor-fails-to-insert-referenc/11147171), [feature ticket 2](https://developercommunity.visualstudio.com/t/Support-for-Cross-Document-Anchor-Links/10993308) to share your feedback and continue the conversation.*

### GitHub Copilot

**Manage Copilot instruction files ð£**
> *The new Copilot Chat experience brings repository and organization guidance together with instruction-file browsing in AI Customization.*
>
> In the new Copilot Chat experience, use **AI Customization** to browse instruction files and check the repository and organization guidance available to your session.
>
> ##### Browse instruction files
>
> Find the instruction files available to your Chat session without searching their folders. Open **AI Customization** to browse sources grouped by scope. Filter the table and inspect full-path tooltips. From a source's **...** menu, choose **Edit** to open its file or **Open in File Explorer** to find it on disk.
>
> ![Instruction files with Edit and Open in File Explorer commands](media/18.12/copilot-instruction-file-actions.png)
>
> ##### Use repository instructions
>
> Add your project's coding conventions, build steps, testing guidance, and other repository instructions to `AGENTS.md` at the solution root. Copilot uses those instructions while working in the solution.
>
> If your repository already uses `AGENTS.md` with other coding agents and command-line tools, you no longer need to maintain a separate copy of the same guidance just for Visual Studio. This helps keep Copilot's behavior consistent across your development tools.
>
> ##### Follow organization guidance
>
> New Chat sessions also use your organization's Copilot custom instructions, so you don't need to copy shared organization guidance into each repository. Visual Studio refreshes that guidance in running and resumed sessions when it changes, and removes old guidance when the organization clears it.
>
> Custom agents receive organization instructions too. The instruction-source list explains when custom instructions are disabled, so you can distinguish missing guidance from a disabled preference.
>
> ð£ *See [feature ticket](https://developercommunity.visualstudio.com/t/Add-support-for-AGENTSmd-files-for-copi/10979070) to share your feedback and continue the conversation.*


**Manage Copilot skills**
> *The new Copilot Chat experience adds individual skill controls in AI Customization.*
>
> In the new Copilot Chat experience, open **AI Customization** to review skills discovered in your solution, repository, user folders, and built-in locations without searching each folder yourself. Workspace discovery follows the active Chat session.
>
> Enable or disable individual skills to choose which ones Copilot can use. Visual Studio saves those choices for later sessions, and built-in skills start disabled so you can decide which to enable. In new Chat sessions, these per-skill controls replace the previous experience's single **Enable Skills** preference.
>
> Use a skill's **...** menu to edit its `SKILL.md` file or open its folder in File Explorer.
>
> ![Skill enablement controls and a menu for editing the skill file](media/18.12/copilot-skill-file-actions.png)


**Manage Copilot MCP servers**
> *The new Copilot Chat experience lets you manage MCP tools, assets, configuration, and authentication in AI Customization.*
>
> In the new Copilot Chat experience, use **MCP Servers** in **AI Customization** to manage the tools and assets available to your session and configure server connections.
>
> ##### Inspect MCP tools and assets
>
> Open **MCP Servers** in **AI Customization** to search a server's tools and enable or disable them individually. Disabled tools stay visible so you can turn them back on. Separate pages show the server's prompts, resources, and read-only instructions.
>
> ![MCP server tools with search and individual enablement controls](media/18.12/copilot-mcp-management-1.png)
>
> ![MCP server prompts with argument and resource descriptions](media/18.12/copilot-mcp-management-2.png)
>
> ##### Configure and add MCP servers
>
> Edit configuration inputs on the server's **Inputs** page and select **Save**. Open the server's configuration file when it has one, or revoke saved authentication even when the server is offline. Built-in servers and non-file sources don't offer an editable configuration file.
>
> To add a server, select the plus button on **MCP Servers**. It opens the existing add-server dialog, so configuration and validation follow the same workflow without returning to the previous tool picker.
>
> ![Add custom MCP server dialog with transport and command fields](media/18.12/copilot-add-server-dialog.png)


**Configure Copilot model connections ð£**
> *Copilot Chat model management adds API-format choices, multiple provider connections, and searchable Microsoft Foundry pickers.*
>
> Copilot Chat's model-management experience gives you more control over connections to models you bring yourself.
>
> ##### Choose a model's API format
>
> When adding a custom model, use **Model API format** to select the request format your endpoint supports: **Completions** or **Responses** for supported non-Anthropic providers, or **Messages** for Anthropic. Choosing a format doesn't add capabilities to the endpoint; it must support the requests and tools you use.
>
> Existing configurations migrate to the provider's default format: **Messages** for Anthropic and **Completions** for other providers. Check the format when connecting to a deployment that expects the Responses API.
>
> ![Add custom model form with the Model API format selector](media/18.12/copilot-model-api-format-selector.png)
>
> ##### Keep multiple provider connections
>
> Add more than one configuration for the same provider, keeping separate endpoints or accounts without replacing your existing connection. Each configuration has its own identity and credentials, so model lookup keeps those connections separate. Existing configurations migrate without requiring you to recreate them.
>
> ![Model management listing multiple configurations for a provider](media/18.12/copilot-multiple-model-connections-1.png)
>
> Enter a **Configuration name** when adding a provider to distinguish connections, such as separate work and personal accounts.
>
> ![Provider configuration form with a name, API key, and endpoint](media/18.12/copilot-provider-configuration.png)
>
> ##### Search Microsoft Foundry pickers
>
> During Microsoft Foundry setup, search inside the subscription and resource dropdowns instead of scrolling through every entry. Resource filtering matches both name and location, and typing a filter preserves the active selection. Your account's existing access permissions still apply.
>
> ![Subscription picker with its search field filtering the list](media/18.12/copilot-foundry-subscription-search.png)
>
> ![Microsoft Foundry resource picker filtered by resource name](media/18.12/copilot-foundry-resource-search.png)
>
> ð£ *See [feature ticket 1](https://developercommunity.visualstudio.com/t/Copilot-BYOM:-Foundry-gpt-6-astra-fails-/11148011), [feature ticket 2](https://developercommunity.visualstudio.com/t/Custom-URLs-for-Models-in-Copilot-Chat/10956896) to share your feedback and continue the conversation.*


**A more capable Copilot Chat ð£**
> *The new Copilot Chat experience adds independent session modes, editor context, trusted paths, multiple session tabs, and a shared user-agent folder.*
>
> The new Copilot Chat experience is now the default for eligible accounts in Visual Studio. It respects an explicit choice to disable editor preview features in your account.
>
> Use Copilot to investigate unfamiliar code, implement features, fix bugs, refactor across files, and work through longer tasks with less back-and-forth. The new experience also improves performance during longer sessions and gives you more ways to customize how Copilot works.
>
> Behind the scenes, it's built on the Copilot SDK, the shared foundation used by the Copilot CLI and the GitHub Copilot app. This helps Visual Studio benefit more quickly from improvements across Copilot while continuing to provide an experience designed for Visual Studio developers.
>
> ![The new Copilot chat experience in Visual Studio](media/18.12/new-chat-experience-18.12.png)
>
> ##### Attach files to your prompt
>
> Drag one or more files from **Windows File Explorer** or **Solution Explorer** into Chat to attach them to your prompt instead of opening them in the editor. Images attach as files too, using the same attachment workflow as the **+** button.
>
> ![Dragging two files into a Copilot Chat prompt](media/18.12/chat-drop-two-files-into-chat.gif)
>
> ##### Generate tests with the Test agent
>
> Choose **Test** from the agent picker to generate tests in the new Chat experience. You need Copilot and its testing capability enabled. The agent follows your selected Chat experience; returning to the previous experience also returns to its previous testing agent.
>
> ##### Choose conversation and tool modes separately
>
> Choose **Interactive** for the usual request-and-response flow or **Autopilot** to keep working until the agent considers the task complete. Select **Manual** or **Allow all** independently for tool permissions.
>
> With **Autopilot** and **Manual** together, tools that aren't configured for automatic approval are rejected rather than waiting for a prompt. Choosing **Allow all** shows a warning. Visual Studio saves these modes with the session and restores them when you return; you can also configure defaults in Options.
>
> Use **Configure Defaults** from the mode menu to open the Chat settings for **Default Conversation Mode** and **Default Tool Permissions**.
>
> ![Chat settings and mode menu with independent conversation and permission defaults](media/18.12/copilot-session-mode-defaults.png)
>
> ##### Keep session context available
>
> Open multiple Chat sessions in separate tabs without replacing the conversation currently in view. Pop-outs are enabled by default in the new experience, and each tab keeps its own conversation.
>
> Copilot can also receive your active file, cursor or selection, file length, and visible line range. Settings control whether to include editor context with requests and whether to refresh it before tool calls. This helps Copilot follow your location if you navigate while it works, without repeating unchanged context.
>
> ##### Manage Copilot trusted paths
>
> The **Trust** settings page now includes a separate list of Copilot trusted paths. Add the working paths you want Copilot to trust without changing the rest of Visual Studio's workspace trust choices.
>
> Copilot no longer inherits trust merely because a workspace is trusted, a path is in a well-known location, or the general trust service is disabled. Your Copilot choices persist through settings, and organizations can manage them through policy.
>
> ##### Use the shared user-agent folder
>
> Visual Studio now creates and discovers user custom agents in `%USERPROFILE%\.copilot\agents` by default, matching Copilot CLI. It no longer defaults to `%USERPROFILE%\.github\agents`.
>
> Visual Studio doesn't move existing agent files. If you used the previous default folder, move your agent files to the new folder or explicitly set the user-agent directory to `%USERPROFILE%\.github\agents` in Visual Studio settings. If you've already configured a custom directory, that setting stays unchanged. Workspace agents remain in your repository's `.github\agents` folder.
>
> ##### Help us improve
>
> We'd love your feedback. If something is missing or not working, send it through **Help â Send Feedback â Report a Problem** so we know what to prioritize next.
>
> If needed, you can return to the previous experience by turning off **Use new Copilot chat experience** under **Tools â Options â GitHub â Copilot â Copilot Chat**, then restarting Visual Studio.
>
> ð£ *See [feature ticket](https://developercommunity.visualstudio.com/t/Drag-and-Drop-to-add-file-reference-in-G/10932863) to share your feedback and continue the conversation.*

### Performance

**A more responsive Visual Studio**
> *Spend less time loading and closing large solutions, opening designers and dialogs, or refreshing status and diagnostics.*
>
> Visual Studio reduces repeated work when loading and closing large solutions, opening designers and dialogs, and refreshing the UI. You don't need to enable new settings to benefit.
>
> ##### Open large C++ solutions faster
>
> Visual Studio reuses project-directory information while refreshing C++ comment tasks and removes an expensive, unused telemetry query during solution opening. In the PR's test scenarios, the measured **Parse Solution** phase took about 20% less time for Chromium and 9% less for Unreal Engine. These figures describe that phase, not a guaranteed reduction in total solution-load time.
>
> ##### Close large solutions with less waiting
>
> Closing a solution no longer scans every open document again for each project it removes. Visual Studio also avoids repeated file-watch cleanup and unnecessary activation of cached C++ projects during teardown. These changes reduce the work required to close solutions with many projects and tracked files.
>
> ##### Keep source-control refreshes responsive
>
> Large source-control status changes can refresh many Solution Explorer icons at once. Visual Studio now processes that work in bounded batches, letting the UI render between batches instead of waiting for every pending icon update. You keep the same status indicators and Git workflow.
>
> ![Solution Explorer refreshing source-control status icons](media/18.12/solution-source-control-icon-performance-1.gif)
>
> ##### Refresh large Error List result sets faster
>
> Legacy diagnostic providers now avoid repeatedly inserting each result into a sorted collection when refreshing the Error List. This reduces UI work when a provider reports many items at once. The change preserves the diagnostics and targets this legacy-provider path, not every diagnostic source.
>
> ##### Open Add New Item with less waiting
>
> When you open **Add New Item**, Visual Studio loads template registrations and caches for the current project family first. It no longer initializes every registered project type before showing the dialog.
>
> You keep the same template choices, project-switching behavior, and user-template refresh. This changes when Visual Studio does the work, not which templates your project can use.
>
> ![Add New Item displaying templates for a .NET console project](media/18.12/add-new-item-dialog-performance-1.png)
>
> ##### Reduce designer startup work
>
> * **Windows Forms:** Complex designers no longer repeat the same registry and loader discovery for every native wrapper object. Visual Studio reuses activation setup on the relevant thread while still creating a fresh wrapper for each object. The improvement targets setup overhead, not your form's initialization code.
> * **UWP XAML:** The designer reuses framework dependency identities already resolved from SDK manifests instead of reopening and parsing complete app packages for the same information. The path-based check remains available when an identity is incomplete. This targets UWP designer startup, not every XAML project type.

### Debugging & diagnostics

**Debug crash dumps with Copilot**
> *Investigate crashes and hangs faster with Copilot analysis directly from the dump summary page.*
>
> Get a head start on investigating crashes and hangs with Debug with Copilot for dump debugging.
>
> Open a dump file in Visual Studio and select **Debug with Copilot** from the **Debug** tab on the dump summary page. Visual Studio starts the dump-debugging session and automatically launches Copilot analysis, helping you understand the captured state and investigate likely causes without manually starting a separate Copilot conversation.
>
> Copilot tailors the initial analysis to the available context: analyzing an exception, investigating an async hang when the main thread is waiting on a task, or providing a general debugging analysis.
>
> ![showing Debug with Copilot option in dump debugging](media/18.12/dump-debug-with-copilot.png)
>
> For the best results, open the matching solution and make the corresponding source files and symbols available to Visual Studio.


**Inspect debugger state through MCP**
> *Visual Studio Debugger MCP adds conditional breakpoints and structured inspection of frame locals and arguments.*
>
> Visual Studio Debugger MCP gives agents more precise ways to stop execution and inspect the values available in a debug frame.
>
> ##### Set conditional breakpoints
>
> Configure expression and hit-count conditions on source and function breakpoints, including combinations with logpoints. An agent can stop only when a condition is met or collect targeted information instead of interrupting on every hit.
>
> Conditions work across launch, attach, continue, and breakpoint updates. If evaluating a condition fails, the debugger still stops and reports the error. Condition syntax depends on the debugger adapter.
>
> ##### Inspect locals and arguments
>
> The `debugger_get_locals` tool returns arguments and local variables for a selected stopped stack frame. Results include names, types, values or evaluation diagnostics, and whether each value can be expanded.
>
> Agents can discover the frame's available values before choosing what to inspect next, rather than guessing expression names. The tool reports unavailable or failed evaluations; it doesn't imply that every value can be evaluated in every debugging state.

### Git tooling

**Open solution filters from TFVC**
> *Find and open solution filters through Source Control Explorer and Team Explorer.*
>
> If you use solution filters to work with a subset of a large solution, you can now reach those filters through TFVC's solution-navigation workflow.
>
> Open a `.slnf` file from **Source Control Explorer**, or find solution filters alongside solutions on the Team Explorer page. You can keep the filter in source control and reach it through the same navigation workflow as the rest of your solution.
>
> Visual Studio recognizes the file as a solution filter, not a standalone solution. Regular solution files keep their existing behavior.


**Resolve Git conflicts with AI**
> *Use AI to resolve Git conflicts, then understand, review, and refine the proposed resolutions.*
>
> Copilot can now resolve Git conflicts for you, starting from **Auto Resolve** in **Git Changes**, the merge editor, or the **Merge branches** dialog. The merge editor can also display resolutions made in your working directory, helping you understand and review conflict resolutions.
>
> ##### Resolve existing conflicts
>
> When you start a merge in Visual Studio, it checks for potential conflicts. You can choose **Auto Resolve** from the **Merge branches** dialog. If there are no conflicts, no requests will be sent, and no tokens will be spent.
>

**MSVC Build Tools 14.52: C++23 complete and more**
> *Try out MSVC Build Tools 14.52 with production-ready C++23 support, optimization improvements, and bug fixes.*
>
> Microsoft C++ (MSVC) Build Tools version 14.52 is shipping in Visual Studio 2026 version 18.12. The new MSVC packages shipping in the Visual Studio Insiders Channel in October 2026 are considered the release candidate, and will be considered stable and fully supported when they reach the Visual Studio Stable Channel in November.
>
> With this release, C++23 is ready for production use and available through the /std:c++23 compiler option; see below for details. MSVC Build Tools v14.52 is now the default toolset installed with C++ workloads. To check if it's installed simply make sure one or both of these components are checked in the installer:
>
> 1. MSVC Build Tools for x64/x86 (Latest)
> 2. MSVC Build Tools for ARM64/ARM64EC (Latest)
>
> You can also select the MSVC components in the installer explicitly labelled with the 14.52 version.
>
> The version number printed by cl.exe and link.exe will be at least 14.52.37025 / 19.52.37025.
>
> We appreciate any feedback that you may have. Please report any issues on [Visual Studio Developer Community](https://developercommunity.visualstudio.com/cpp).
>
> This release includes changes across the compiler frontend, backend, linker, standard library, and related tools since MSVC 14.51.
>
> ##### C++ standards conformance
>
> * **C++23 language mode:** Use `/std:c++23` to select C++23 language rules. The existing `/std:c++23preview` spelling still works and is an alias for `/std:c++23`. The preview form is now deprecated and will be removed in a future update.
> * **Immediate escalation:** C++23 immediate escalation (P2564R3) lets eligible `constexpr` functions and lambdas become immediate when their use requires it. It is enabled in C++23 and later modes; C++20 builds can opt in with `/Zc:immediateEscalation`.
> * **Unicode identifiers:** C++23 and C23 modes recognize the mathematical compatibility identifier ranges from P3658R1.
> * **Constexpr allocation in modules:** Module interfaces can represent `constexpr` functions that contain `new T[n]` expressions.
> * **Preprocessor behavior:** `_Pragma` works in more macro-expansion cases and is supported under `/E`.
> * **Constexpr cmath:** Support for C++ compile-time cmath functions remains off-by-default under /std:c++23 and may be enabled via the /Zc:cmath switch. Please see <https://devblogs.microsoft.com/cppblog/msvc-c23-constexpr-cmath-with-llvm-libc/> for additional details.
>
> ##### C++/CLI, C, and language tooling
>
> * `/clr` is now available in C++23 and later modes.
> * The opt-in `/Zc:functionToObjectPtr` switch rejects implicit conversions from function pointers to `void*`.
> * The compiler now accepts selected `constexpr` constructor-template instantiations involving virtual base classes. Constructing those virtual bases during constant evaluation remains unsupported, so this is limited to the declaration checks for a `constexpr` function.
> * In C code, C4815 and C4816 now warn when a structure is allocated without storage for its flexible array member or when a structure with a flexible array member is passed by value.
> * The Linux C++ IntelliSense parser maps C++20 and C++23 standard options to the corresponding language modes.
> * Argument-dependent lookup now handles more names that are not exported from a module, and nested template and module instantiation is less prone to failure.
> * Module serialization preserves class data members and template information more consistently. Type merging also works better when several modules share a header unit.
> * Header units preserve macro whitespace so stringized macros survive a round trip. Module processing also handles types first defined in the global module fragment more reliably.
> * Math intrinsics and math headers now work more consistently with modules and constant evaluation.
> * Caret diagnostics use less memory, and several diagnostics reproduce the original source expression more accurately.
> * Preprocessor diagnostics better identify malformed and nested constant expressions.
> * The compiler handles invalid type-trait inputs and malformed function-parameter scopes more consistently.
> * The compiler warns when overriding a deprecated non-pure virtual function.
>
> ##### Code generation and optimization
>
> **Inlining:**
>
> * LTCG now considers which fields of a small return object the caller reads, so inlining can discard work that computes unused fields.
> * Whole-program optimization can favor an inline when doing so exposes parts of a local object and makes unused stores removable.
> * A large outlined loop body can now inline through a small wrapper called from a loop.
> * With PGO, small size-optimized virtual-call targets can be speculatively inlined when the profile, size, and growth limits allow it.
> * The inliner follows function-pointer values through aggregate assignments, preserving more indirect-call opportunities in template adapters.
> * Type-based devirtualization now works alongside profile-guided inlining. Hot/cold information also does more to prevent cold code from being pulled into hot callers.
>
> **Loop and scalar optimization:**
>
> * The compiler can move more invariant loads out of loops after proving that each load executes on every iteration and remains safe across aliased pointers.
> * Equality-tested loops shed more loop-carried work, and strength reduction handles more wrapping integer induction expressions.
> * When three or more multiplications share a divisor, the optimizer can compute one reciprocal and reuse it instead of restoring repeated divisions.
> * Copy propagation through aliased fields is on by default and understands known-size `memcpy` and `memset` operations.
> * x64 conditional selection handles more nonzero constants and safe aliased operands.
> * Unsigned comparisons and induction-variable ranges now establish more nonzero, ordering, and non-overflow facts for later optimization.
> * Scalar conditional expressions gain more value-equivalence, incoming-value, multiply, and shift simplifications.
> * Calls use `restrict` arguments more precisely when determining memory interference, exposing more optimization around those calls.
> * The x86 optimizer performs more local and cross-block copy propagation.
> * The compiler recognizes more rotate idioms and dynamic bit-field extraction controls, and removes redundant POPCNT zero extension.
> * Small-aggregate optimization removes padding-only assignments, decomposes qualifying whole-struct loads, and forwards eligible loads through local `memcpy` operations.
> * Constant conversions can fold without `/fp:fast` when the transformation is otherwise valid.
> * Earlier loop-invariant motion and broader expression reassociation expose more work to later optimization.
> * Larger functions reuse more repeated expressions. Min/max expressions, mixed-signedness compare diamonds, and repeated vector-element extraction also simplify in more cases.
> * More indirect calls to `noexcept` functions become tail calls. Static constant arrays can also disappear when their storage is unnecessary.
> * Loop unswitching handles more nested-loop cases before vectorization, while straight-line vectorization handles more merged values.
> * Jump chains and induction variables simplify in more cases without losing useful predicates or signedness information.
> * The compiler emits less attribute data, scans exception regions fewer times, bounds pathological dead-use searches, and processes large chained function expressions in linear rather than quadratic time.
>
> **Vectorization:**
>
> * On x64 and ARM64, the compiler vectorizes more code that selects values through branches.
> * Integer reductions such as `sum += a[i] - b[i]` can be reassociated into a form the loop vectorizer recognizes.
> * On x64 and ARM64, vector loads and stores reach copy propagation and scalar replacement earlier. Full-width vectors remain intact when splitting them would discard useful vector operations.
> * The vectorizer recognizes more adjacent-address patterns and is more willing to pack user-written SIMD values when the result can remain in a vector register.
> * A parameter-derived pointer advanced by a loop is recognized as non-aliasing a local array in more cases, avoiding an unnecessary runtime overlap check.
> * The loop vectorizer handles qualifying memory-only swaps and multi-stream copies, including `std::swap` on arrays of trivial types.
> * More loop-control expressions shared by a following conditional simplify after the loop.
>
> ##### ARM64
>
> * ARM64 now shares address calculations across related loads and stores, including array-of-structures loops based on function parameters. This removes repeated arithmetic and creates more opportunities for paired loads and stores.
> * Known NEON constants can be built without unnecessary data loads. Scalar loads, broadcasts, and lane inserts also fold into NEON load instructions in more cases.
> * The compiler combines more NEON construction and lane operations, removes unused lane inserts, and eliminates redundant mask comparisons.
> * The loop vectorizer now handles additional `floor`, `ceil`, `trunc`, and `round` operations.
> * Tail-call decisions are now made per call, so one ineligible call no longer blocks another eligible call in the same function.
> * ARM64 and ARM64EC inlining accounts for floating-point and vector register pressure. This preserves profitable native ARM64 inlines while avoiding excessive spills on restricted ARM64EC targets.
> * Native ARM64 SVE2 supports code generation and disassembly for lane-indexed `svmullb` and `svmullt` intrinsics. Execution requires SVE2-capable hardware.
> * LUTI2 and LUTI4 lookup-table support includes BF16 forms. Floating-point absolute minimum/maximum instructions and Common Short Sequence Compression operations are also supported. Each family requires the corresponding processor feature.
> * `ARM64_FPMR` names the FPMR register for `_ReadStatusReg` and `_WriteStatusReg`; armasm64 and the disassembler recognize the same name. Execution requires FEAT\_FPMR hardware and OS permission.
> * Native ARM64 supports `__preserve_none` and `[[msvc::musttail]]`, including specialized interpreter dispatch. The `__preserve_none` calling convention is C-only and is not supported on ARM64EC.
> * With `/feature:sme`, the compiler accepts SME attributes and ZA-state types on supported external declarations. Eligible scalar `noexcept` calls can perform the required streaming-mode transitions, including selected function-pointer, reference, whole-program, and Control Flow Guard cases. Streaming function definitions, ZA-bearing calls, unsupported pointer forms, and vector or aggregate arguments remain unsupported. ARM64EC is excluded.
> * The native ARM64 CRT supplies the AAPCS64 SME state-management routines for TPIDR2, ZA, and ZT0. Availability depends on processor and operating-system state support; ARM64EC is excluded.
> * On ARM64, the `/Zc:cmath` math runtime now supports the floating-point environment. This initial implementation reports math errors through floating-point exceptions rather than `errno`.
> * ARM64 stack layout can reuse slots for locals in mutually exclusive switch cases, greatly reducing the frame size of large switches.
> * Stateless SVE all-true predicates can move out of loops when the usual safety and profitability checks allow it.
> * Proven-dead switch edges are removed before switch expansion, exposing more control-flow and value optimizations.
> * Bitfield operations use narrower immediate forms where possible.
> * Register assignment preserves more adjacent load pairs and makes better spill/rematerialization choices for frequently used values.
> * Used-lane tracking now crosses more scalar floating-point operations, exposing dead vector work.
> * The compiler recognizes more vector permutations, per-lane rotations, and vector bit-clear immediate forms.
> * SVE comparisons and the MATCH/NMATCH/WHILE families reuse condition flags more effectively. NEON-to-SVE bridge moves, upper-lane float extraction, and by-element multiply addressing also produce shorter sequences.
>
> ##### x64 and x86
>
> * Speed-optimized x64 builds have more strategies for fixed-length `memcmp`. Eligible copies larger than 256 bytes use the runtime copy path instead of a large inline sequence.
> * x64 removes more redundant zero extensions before jump-table address calculations and lowers unsigned division by a constant power of two to a shift.
> * Constant `f64x2` assignments can combine so a later vector operation folds to one 128-bit constant move.
> * 32-bit x86 builds can inline `fmin`, `fmax`, and `copysign`; ARM64 can inline `copysign`.
> * AVX2 and AVX-512 targets can build wider vectors from smaller register values without a memory round trip.
> * AVX-512 code generation uses suitable VEX moves for intrinsic operands and folds eligible single-use masked arithmetic followed by a blend into one merge-masked operation.
> * Builds using `/feature:APX` gain more arithmetic and conditional-selection forms, fewer redundant moves and comparisons, and APX-aware unrolling and strength-reduction decisions for scalar integer loops.
> * APX support now spans the ABI, assembler, disassembler, and debugging tools. R30 and R31 are nonvolatile, register assignment treats them as killed across `setjmp`, MASM and the disassembler handle eligible extended-register encodings, and DIA reads APX register context.
> * APX-enabled x64 code generation can fold eligible operands and makes better spill, recomputation, and fold choices.
> * Unwind V3 support now spans code generation, linking, ML64, DIA, and binary instrumentation. It covers chained runtime-function records, large prologs and epilogs, `.PUSHFRAME`/`.POPFRAME`, and stack walking. ML64 requires `/unwindv3`; compiler emission is on by default only for APX functions, and stack walking requires a V3-aware operating system and debugger.
> * x64 recognizes more condition-code-safe `INC`/`DEC` forms, including eligible atomic fetch-add sequences.
> * AVX2 intrinsic lowering removes unnecessary scalar-to-vector moves in qualifying `_mm_set_sd` and `_mm256_set1_pd` paths.
> * APX code generation includes more new-destination and memory-operand forms, shorter LEA replacements for eligible INC/DEC and SUB sequences, and broader shift, compare, conditional-compare, conditional-move, and constant-propagation support.
> * All-bits-set vector constants and functions containing paired register operations receive better code generation.
> * Shift-range analysis models the hardware shift-count mask, and adjacent two-element double stores combine more effectively.
> * Under `/O1` and `/Os`, additional pre-allocation optimizations and size-aware instruction costs reduce code size.
> * RDPRU uses its required fixed-register constraints.
>
> ##### Standard Library
>
> See the [STL Changelog - MSVC Build Tools 14.52](https://github.com/microsoft/STL/wiki/Changelog#msvc-build-tools-1452) for a complete list of all of the changes in this release, grouped by features, LWG issue resolutions, bug fixes, performance improvements, etc. Some highlights:

>
> * Improved runtime performance by removing duplicated quarantine work

To trace what instructions were intercepted by MSDIS instead of the manual instruction decoder, set verbosity=3 and search for logs prefixed with "MSDIS instruction decoder:".

> ##### Build tools and diagnostics
>
> * The C++ frontend accepts more valid designated-initialization forms.
> * The C++ frontend accepts more deeply nested initializers, and the legacy preprocessor allows larger macro buffers.
> * Code Analysis SARIF output includes rule names, descriptions, and help links by default, plus tags where available.
> * LNK2022 and LNK4227 name the relevant metadata item. LNK4323 explains a missing ARM64EC/native object pair.
> * Incremental linking trims excess growth space from program-database files.
> * The disassembly library recognizes MIPS32 and MIPS64 Release 6 instructions and ARM64 matrix-state start/stop instructions.
> * `/analyze:log:format:sarifandxml` writes both Code Analysis log formats.
> * LNK4321 identifies duplicate C++ module exports while generating an import library.
> * C5089 identifies the experimental combination of `/fsanitize=address` with `/clr`, including `/clr:netcore`.
> * In C++, two new level-4 warnings diagnose implicit and explicit conversions between `HRESULT`/`SCODE` and `bool`-like types. They are off by default and do not apply to C.
> * The opt-in `/PDB4GBSTREAMS` option raises the size limit for the PDB global/public symbol-record stream to roughly 4 GiB. Other PDB streams retain their existing limits.
> * MASM and the disassembly library recognize the x86 `int1`/ICEBP instruction (`0xF1`).
> * LTCG emits C4744 when `extern` declarations disagree on type.
> * PE reproducibility improves because the image hash no longer includes the PDB age.
> * Tag-based Code Analysis warning groups simplify ruleset authoring.
> * Debugger clients can release a program-database file handle without discarding loaded data, allowing the file to be rebuilt sooner. Debug information also merges module and header-unit types more reliably.
> * Debug records can identify alternate object names, and type-record processing performs fewer allocations and improves throughput on large programs.
> * Linker and assembler diagnostics are clearer, and malformed object files, libraries, and module metadata are handled more defensively.

**Reduce UI work during CMake project discovery**
> *Repeated CMake project scans no longer trigger duplicate project-discovery notifications.*
>
> Removed duplicate project-discovery notifications from repeated scans of a CMake workspace, reducing unnecessary UI-thread work during project discovery.
>
> Open or refresh your CMake project as usual. Visual Studio still reports newly discovered project providers, without repeatedly reporting the same provider within that workspace.


**C++ Dynamic Debugging leaves Preview**
> *Debug optimized C++ code with on-demand function deoptimization using a feature that is no longer marked as Preview.*
>
> C++ Dynamic Debugging's Preview labels were removed. You can continue to debug optimized code with on-demand function deoptimization, with updated labels in the project property pages and compiler, linker, and librarian option descriptions.
>
> To use it in an x64 C++ project, open the project properties, set **Configuration Properties â Advanced â Use C++ Dynamic Debugging** to **Yes**, and rebuild. This mode turns off Whole Program Optimization.
>
> See [C++ Dynamic Debugging](/en-us/visualstudio/debugger/cpp-dynamic-debugging) for setup instructions and limitations.


**Reduce CPU work when resolving C++ includes**
> *Visual Studio avoids repeated path processing when resolving include files in large C++ solutions.*
>
> Reduced CPU work when resolving include files while parsing large C++ solutions. The include resolver reuses normalized include paths and cached directory lookups instead of repeating that work for each search.
>
> The improvement applies automatically as Visual Studio parses your C++ code. You do not need to change your project's include directories or enable a new option.


**Avoid hangs during concurrent C++ project updates**
> *A deadlock between C++ project updates and background directory imports was resolved.*
>
> A deadlock that could freeze the IDE when C++ project updates overlapped with background directory imports was resolved. The project system now avoids holding a shared cache lock while accessing the project database.
>
> The fix applies automatically to existing C++ projects, without changes to your project settings.


**Run remote CMake tests more reliably**
> *Test Explorer establishes remote connections before launching CMake tests and retries transient connection failures.*
>
> Fixed cases where **Test Explorer** discovered tests in a remote CMake project but left them as **Not Run** when you tried to run or debug them. Before launching tests, **Test Explorer** now establishes the remote connection and retries transient connection failures.
>
> For an existing CMake project configured for a remote Linux target, select a discovered test in **Test Explorer** and run or debug it as usual. Connection setup also respects cancellation; authentication failures and rejected host keys still require you to resolve the underlying connection issue.


**Avoid false rebuild prompts in Unreal projects ð£**
> *Start debugging an already-built Unreal Engine project without a false out-of-date prompt.*
>
> We fixed a false out-of-date prompt that appeared when you started debugging an already-built Unreal Engine project. Previously, pressing **F5** without changing the project could still prompt you to rebuild.
>
> The fix applies to NMake configurations that do not provide the build-state information required by Visual Studio's built-in up-to-date check, including the affected Unreal Engine projects. Build your project and press **F5** as usual; you do not need to disable up-to-date checks globally.
>
> ð£ *See [feature ticket](https://developercommunity.visualstudio.com/t/Regression:-VS-2026-Fast-Up-to-Date-Chec/11031914) to share your feedback and continue the conversation.*

### Extensibility

**Build extensions for multiple SDK targets ð£**
> *The updated extension compatibility model adds a Visual Studio 2026 SDK, SDK-style project choices, and multi-targeted extension payloads.*
>
> As part of the updated extension compatibility model, you can now build extensions with the first Visual Studio SDK (VSSDK) specifically targeting Visual Studio 2026, version 18.12 and later.
>
> Use the new SDK when your extension needs APIs available in this target. You can also publish extensions built against the new SDK to Visual Studio Marketplace.
>
> If you also support earlier Visual Studio versions, you can use multi-targeted builds to produce a separate payload for each SDK target and publish them under one Marketplace entry. This lets you adopt newer APIs while keeping a compatible payload available for your existing users.
>
> ##### Choose a project build style
>
> In the **Modern VSIX Project** template, clear **Use top-level Visual Studio SDK** to create a regular `Microsoft.NET.Sdk` project with explicit package references. This option supports VSSDK, VisualStudio.Extensibility, and hybrid extensions.
>
> The top-level SDK stays selected by default. The existing C# VSIX Project and Empty VSIX Project templates remain available.
>
> ##### Build a payload for each SDK target
>
> Target multiple Visual Studio SDK versions in one VSIX project. The build tooling supports top-level SDKs and target framework monikers, producing a separate payload for each SDK target declared in `TargetFrameworks`.
>
> ```
> <Project Sdk="Microsoft.VisualStudio.Sdk.Build">
>   <PropertyGroup>
>   <TargetFrameworks>vs17_14;vs18_12</TargetFrameworks>
>   <ExtensionType>VisualStudio.Extensibility</ExtensionType>
>   <LangVersion>latest</LangVersion>
>   </PropertyGroup>
> </Project>
> ```
>
> Your 18.12 payload can use APIs introduced for that target, while the 17.14 payload remains available for compatible earlier installations. Upload and manage these payloads under one Marketplace entry. Multiple payloads are supported for listings that support Visual Studio 2022 or later.
>
> ![Marketplace extension listing offering Visual Studio 2026 and Visual Studio 2022 downloads](media/18.12/extension-marketplace-payloads.png)
>
> ##### Install the matching payload automatically
>
> When you install or update a multi-targeted Marketplace extension, Visual Studio selects the best compatible payload. You still see one extension entry and don't need to choose an SDK target yourself.
>
> For example, with 17.14 and 18.12 payloads available, Visual Studio 17.14 receives the 17.14 payload and Visual Studio 18.12 receives the 18.12 payload. Updates use the same selection logic.
>
> ð£ *See [feature ticket](https://developercommunity.visualstudio.com/t/When-will-MicrosoftVisualStudioInterop/10997805) to share your feedback and continue the conversation.*


**Extension Manager renderings ð£**
> *Read extension descriptions with working animations, clearer tables, and properly rendered headings.*
>
> Extension Manager now renders animated GIFs, tables, and headings correctly in extension descriptions. You can read structured information and watch an extension's animations directly in its description.
>
> Tables now use padding, borders, and alternating row highlights, making their contents easier to scan and compare.
>
> ![Extension Manager description showing a styled table](media/18.12/ext-man-tables.png)
>

Released on November 10, 2026.

IDE

Work in Solution Explorer's File System view

Browse your repository's physical layout, switch solutions, and run project commands from Solution Explorer's File System view.

Solution Explorer's File System view lets you explore your repository's physical layout while keeping solution and project actions within reach.

Browse your repository's physical layout

Switch to File System view to browse files as they exist on disk, including documentation, build assets, and configuration files outside your projects. In a repository, the view starts at the repository root; otherwise, it starts at the solution folder. Switch back to Solution view for project structure, dependencies, and loaded projects.

To keep both layouts visible, choose New Solution Explorer View from the context menu and put Solution and File System views side by side. You don't need a separate window merely to switch views.

Switch solutions from File System view

If your repository contains several solutions, you can open another one without leaving its physical folder layout. Double-click a solution file in File System view, then choose whether to open it in your current Visual Studio instance or a new one.

Run project commands without switching views

Right-click a project in File System view to use Build, Rebuild, Clean, or Set as Startup Project. You can explore files outside the solution and use common project commands from the same view.

These actions apply to projects in the active solution. Projects outside that solution don't enable the build actions.


Restore MSBuild dependencies in Open Folder

Run MSBuild Restore from Open Folder without opening a solution first.

When you work in Open Folder, you can prepare MSBuild dependencies without opening a solution first. Right-click a supported solution or project file and choose Restore to run the MSBuild Restore target through the folder's existing build-action workflow.

For a project that belongs to a discovered solution, the action preserves its solution-specific targeting. This keeps restore in the project's solution context even though you're working from the folder view.

This action doesn't apply to CMake or other build providers, and excludes C++ .vcxproj files.


More settings in updated Options

The updated Options experience includes product-update, Dev Containers, and graphics capture settings without resetting your preferences.

The updated Options experience brings more existing settings into the same interface without resetting your saved preferences.

Manage product updates

Manage Background Downloads, Operation Mode, and supported Update on Close behavior in updated Options. Your existing defaults and saved choices remain, and the installer action is still available.

Controls reflect product capabilities and organizational policy. If policy disables Update on Close, the page retains the explanation instead of presenting a setting you can change.

Find Dev Containers settings

Open Cross Platform â Dev Containers in updated Options to manage existing container preferences. Your saved settings and host selection stay synchronized with the existing store; you don't need to recreate your container setup. This integration ships with the CMake Linux extension.

Configure graphics captures

The seven existing graphics Capture controls now appear in updated Options. Compatibility mode and HUD options use positive labels, and the page updates when another process changes the shared capture values. The migrated page replaces the legacy placeholder rather than showing two competing pages.

ANSI colors in the Output window ð£

Render ANSI-colored tool output without raw escape sequences obscuring messages.

If a tool emits ANSI-colored messages, you can now read those colors directly in the Output window instead of seeing raw escape sequences mixed into the text.

Enable colorized output in Visual Studio's visual-experience settings to try it. The option starts disabled, so you keep verbatim output until you choose color rendering.

When you enable the option, Visual Studio removes escape sequences from the displayed text and preserves their color transitions. Selection, copying, and searching then use the visible text, not the hidden sequences.

Leave the option off if you need the original output exactly as the tool emitted it, including escape sequences.

Language-server hover tips show syntax-colored signatures and examples in a compact view that covers less of your code.

Hover tips from language servers now show fenced code in compact, syntax-colored views instead of large generic panels. Signatures and examples take less space over the editor, and the prominent Copy Code control is removed.

Markdown links and keyboard navigation still work. The embedded code is a read-only display, not another editor that takes focus or offers text selection. This applies to language-server hover content, not every Quick Info provider.

Preview more image formats ð£

Solution Explorer previews more image formats, including TIFF, DDS, and WebP, without opening an editor.

Hover over an image in Solution Explorer to preview TIFF, DDS, JPEG XR, HD Photo, Windows Media Photo, or WebP, alongside existing PNG, JPEG, GIF, BMP, and ICO support. Previews also work in Open Folder, matching the formats available in the editor.

Some formats, including WebP, may require the appropriate Windows image codecs.

Tab and window management improvements ð£

Customize tool-window tabs, close tabs to the right, and cancel accidental window drags.

Customize tool-window tabs

Choose how much space tool-window tabs can use by setting their minimum and maximum widths. Go to Tools â Options â Environment â Tabs â Tool Window Tabs to customize the limits.

Before

After

Tool-window tabs shrink to their content size and your minimum width before truncating labels with an ellipsis and shrinking all tabs uniformly.

Tool-window tabs also use a consistent 24-pixel height, show clearer drag feedback, and improve high-contrast behavior.

Close tabs to the right

Right-click a document tab or a tool window docked in the document well and select Close Tabs to the Right. With vertical tabs, choose Close Tabs Below instead. The command follows visible tab order, keeps pinned and unpinned groups separate, and leaves preview tabs open.

Cancel a window drag

While dragging a docked window, press Esc before releasing the mouse button. Visual Studio cancels the drag and returns the window to its previous docked position.

Syntax highlighting and TextMate updates

Read more file types with improved syntax highlighting and try a faster Preview TextMate matcher.

Visual Studio's editor improves syntax colors across more file types. TextMate matching also gains a separate Preview option.

Edit TOML and Rust with updated grammars

TOML files now support syntax highlighting, code folding, brace completion, and comment/uncomment commands through a new TextMate grammar.

The updated Rust TextMate grammar improves syntax highlighting and recognizes newer Rust language features.

Read registry and solution files more easily

Registry (.reg) and package-definition (.pkgdef) files now highlight comments, sections, assignments, strings, deletion syntax, and typed values. Package-definition highlighting also recognizes qword: values and #include directives. Solution files gain highlighting for their structure too.

Try faster TextMate matching

Enable Use faster TextMate grammar matching in Preview Features to try the new matcher. It searches eligible grammar rules together and keeps the existing matcher for unsupported cases.

In a local benchmark using one 1.09 MB TypeScript fixture, parsing fell from 8.989 seconds to 1.882 seconds. This result describes that fixture, not a guaranteed improvement for every file. The matcher doesn't replace the JavaScript or TypeScript language service.

Productivity

Control inline suggestions in comments ð£

Turn off automatic inline suggestions in comments without disabling them in code.

Turn off automatic inline suggestions in comments without disabling them in code. Open Tools â Options â Text Editor â Preferences and clear Show suggestions in comments.

The preference starts enabled to preserve existing behavior and includes C# XML documentation and C++ comments. You can still explicitly request completion in a comment when you want it.

Display editor guides at configured columns to follow your repository's line-length conventions.

The editor adds line guides so you can follow your repository's configured line lengths while writing.

Use rulers to display one or more guides:

rulers = 80, 120

When rulers isn't specified, Visual Studio falls back to max_line_length:

max_line_length = 120

If both properties are present, rulers takes precedence. Set either property to unset to suppress an inherited value. The guide color follows the Visual Studio theme and can be customized through Tools â Options â Environment â Fonts and Colors.

Markdown links and heading navigation ð£

Create Markdown links by dragging files and follow links directly to headings in other documents.

Adding links and images to Markdown is now as easy as drag and drop. Drag a file from Solution Explorer or Windows File Explorer onto the Markdown editor, and Visual Studio inserts the correct Markdown syntax at the drop location. Regular files become links, while supported image files become image references.

Visual Studio handles the path details for you.
